Food diary — how to keep one and what to bring to a dietitian

Updated: 2026-09-04 7 min read

A food diary is the simplest diagnostic tool in nutrition and also the one most often kept badly. Below: what to log, for how long, and what specifically a dietitian is trying to read out of it.

In this guide

  1. Why logging alone changes something
  2. What to log and what to skip
  3. For how many days
  4. What a dietitian actually wants to see
  5. Five mistakes that ruin a diary
  6. When to stop logging

Why logging alone changes something

Before anyone analyses the diary, it is already doing work. The phenomenon is well described in health psychology as self-monitoring: knowing an action will be recorded changes the action.

In practice that means the second biscuit stops being a reflex and becomes a decision — because it will have to be written down. This is not about guilt. It is that some eating happens outside conscious attention, and a record puts the attention back.

It is also why a diary kept honestly for two weeks usually shows intake falling — even when nobody prescribed any change. Worth remembering when interpreting it: the first week tends to be unusually well behaved.

What to log and what to skip

The most common reason diaries get abandoned is trying to record everything at maximum precision. After four days it becomes a second job. A workable split looks like this:

Always logLog if you canSkip
Every mealApproximate weightsCalories calculated by hand
Snacks, down to one square of chocolateThe time of the mealBrand names
Every drink except plain waterHunger before, fullness after (1–5)Micronutrients
Fats added during cookingMood and sleepStep-by-step recipes
AlcoholPhysical activityPerfect precision

The first column is mandatory, because without it the diary does not describe reality. The second turns a list of food into something you can draw conclusions from — times and hunger levels are what explain why a craving for something sweet turns up at ten in the evening. The third adds nothing that cannot be filled in later.

A photo instead of a description

Typing a meal in takes a minute and requires estimating weights at the exact moment you are hungry and want to eat. A photo takes three seconds. For the completeness of a diary that difference is decisive — estimating from a photo is less accurate than a kitchen scale, but a diary that actually exists beats a more accurate one that does not.

For how many days

It depends on the purpose, and that distinction saves a lot of unnecessary work:

PurposeLengthNote
Diagnosis before seeing a dietitian7 consecutive daysmust include Saturday and Sunday
Establishing your own requirement14 daysalongside daily weighing
Running a fat-loss phasedaily, but brieflycompleteness beats precision
Checking in after a diet ends2–3 days a weekenough to catch drift

The weekend has to be in there. This is the most common flaw in diaries brought to an appointment: five working days look exemplary, while for many people the gap between Saturday and Tuesday runs to a thousand calories. A week without a weekend describes somebody who does not exist.

What a dietitian actually wants to see

Counter to intuition, it is not the calories. A dietitian can total those in a few minutes. What they read from the diary are the things an interview cannot recover, because nobody remembers them:

  • The rhythm of the day. When the first meal happens, how many hours sit between meals, whether most of the energy lands in the evening.
  • How protein is distributed. Spread across the day, or all sitting in dinner.
  • Fruit and vegetables. The number of portions a day, not the claim that you “try to eat healthily”.
  • Fluids. How much and what kind — that alone settles a lot of questions about fatigue and headaches.
  • Patterns, not events. Whether snacking has a time of day, or follows particular situations.
  • Weekday versus weekend. Usually the single largest source of discrepancy.

What form to bring it in

Ideally as one PDF or printout, in chronological order, with dates and times. Screenshots from an app are fine too, as long as the dates are visible. What to avoid: loose sheets, notes spread across several places, and an export in a format nobody can open without that same app.

If your app supports exporting the diary, export a full week and check whether the file contains photos or meal descriptions — a table of calorie totals is far less useful than a list of what was actually on the plate.

Five mistakes that ruin a diary

  1. Writing it up in the evening from memory. After eight hours, 20–30% of what was eaten has disappeared on average. Log at the moment of eating or immediately after.
  2. Leaving out caloric drinks. Juice, a latte, a beer, a sports drink — for many people that is 300–600 kcal a day that never reaches the record.
  3. Not counting cooking fats. Two tablespoons of olive oil is about 240 kcal. It is the single most frequently omitted item in any diary.
  4. Eating a “nicer” week for the diary's benefit. If you eat differently for those seven days, you are diagnosing somebody else. The diary is there to describe the starting point, not to make a good impression.
  5. Quitting after a bad day. One unlogged day does not invalidate the week. A gap in the data is far less damaging than an abandoned diary.

When to stop logging

A diary is a tool, not a lifestyle. It is worth keeping for as long as it is still teaching you something.

After a few months most people estimate their own meals markedly better than they did at the start — a skill the diary builds incidentally and which stays once you put it down. At that point it makes sense to drop to two or three days a week: enough to catch drift, without occupying attention day to day.

There is one situation in which the diary should be put down regardless of benefit: if it starts driving anxiety around food, makes eating away from home a problem, or produces a compulsion to “make up for” a worse day. Those are signals that the tool is doing more harm than good — and a moment for a conversation with a professional, not for counting more carefully.

Common questions

How do I keep a food diary?

Log every meal, snack, drink other than water, and any fat added during cooking — at the moment of eating, not in the evening from memory. Add times and hunger levels if you can, because those explain the patterns. You do not need to calculate calories by hand; completeness matters more.

How many days should a food diary cover for a dietitian?

Seven consecutive days, and it must include Saturday and Sunday. Five working days describe somebody who does not exist — for many people the gap between weekend and weekday runs to a thousand calories, and that is usually the most important thing to discuss at the appointment.

What should I bring to a first dietitian appointment?

A seven-day diary with dates and times, ideally as a single PDF or printout, any recent blood work you have, a list of medications and supplements, and your weight history over recent months. A calorie total is less useful than a list of what was actually on the plate.

Does keeping a food diary help you lose weight?

Yes, and before anyone analyses it. Self-monitoring means that knowing something will be recorded changes the behaviour itself — some eating happens outside conscious attention, and the diary restores it. That is why the first week of logging tends to be unusually well behaved.

Do I have to weigh food to keep a diary?

Not at the diagnostic stage — there, completeness matters, not precision. A scale earns its place for a few days when establishing your own requirement, and for calorie-dense foods such as nuts, oils and nut butters, where a 20 g error is an error of over 100 kcal.
